utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to continue its --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone. Yesterday, by the end of the hearing, we broke off when the Defence was speaking, analysing as part of the final closing argument whether there were any proof regarding General Galic's subordinates targeted civilians. Now, the Prosecutor offered the testimony of Witnesses Ashton, Henneberry, Carswell, Gardemeister. When we were assessing these testimonies regarding the allegations they made during their testimony, the Defence would like to point out that the testimony going in this direction were insufficient and did not give any grounds that they should be accepted. Regarding the credibility of the testimony of Henneberry, Carswell, and Gardemeister, the ones that we have mentioned. Particularly when we are speaking about the testimony of Witness Ashton, the Defence would like to point to some details that will bring into question the credibility of this witness as well regarding this matter. In his closing argument, the Prosecutor offered the claim that this witness is an experienced journalist and later on as a humanitarian worker knew how to use photography, and we were also shown a series of photographs. Carefully analysing the photographs, we can doubt the authenticity of this instance filmed if this witness had really been present at some events when civilians were targeted, then he probably would have filmed, he would have recorded this event. However, the witness has no such photographs. We claim that the testimony regarding certain circumstances Witness Ashton is in the realm fantasy. We will give an example of his testimony when he said the Serb fighters had placed, mounted an astronomical telescope on a cannon. Now every cannon as a field gun has its sight which is constructed in such a way to make it possible to successfully fire to the final range, and there is no need to place on it an astronomical telescope. Now, these are just stories, fantastical stories that Witness Ashton told us, and one of the stories was the story of the iron cross regarding which Witness Ashton told us was that this was a pattern, the way the artillery fired, the Serb artillery fired. None of the witnesses who were heard before this Trial Chamber confirmed this, corroborated this testimony. Nor was it mentioned by anyone else. And the Defence believes that if the testimony of Witness Ashton as part of the media propaganda that was waged against the Serbs, then this witness was part of it. So the Defence believes that the evidence offered by the Prosecution did not prove that anybody who was subordinate to General Galic targeted civilians. The Prosecution regarding the command responsibility of General Galic wishes to refer to a good coordination of all the operations of SRK units, but is not referring to evidence that would prove that there was deliberate targeting of civilians by SRK units. This matter regarding good coordination is also to do with the example that illustrates -- that is illustrated by example of the barrage fire, the screened fire, which allegedly took place Christmas Eve 1992 and also at -- on 7th of January, 1993, and 14th of January, at midnight, 1993. And the Prosecution is referring to testimony of Witness Tucker. Now, the Defence claims that this has been countered by the Defence Witness DP35. And at the request of the Trial Chamber, the Defence has shown the annex 6(A) of the UN expert report for the question, and this clearly shows that there was no firing at all, particularly no barrage or screened fire, on those dates. This evidence confirmed that in none of the two days, there was no screened fire in the city, not even during the days when the holidays really are on -- well, not during the days that are erroneously quoted by the Prosecution, like the 14th of January. Now, regarding the testimony of Witnesses Cutler, Harding, and Tucker, regarding the shooting that allegedly took place orthodox new year, we believe that they are mutually contradictory and contrary to evidence shown; they cannot be accepted. All other allegations by the Prosecution that would point to the command responsibility from paragraphs 140 to 164 of the final brief are irrelevant, and we would like to stress that they are just pure theory. There is no evidence there. The Prosecution [as interpreted] will also counter the allegations of the Prosecution claim in paragraph 158 regarding the testimony of Colonel Cutler who spoke of alleged threats of Colonel Marticic that Sarajevo will be fired at if the Bosnians do not stop firing at Ilidza. Ilidza is a part of the Sarajevo battlefield. And according to the Defence, these so-called threats are just usual in the domain of negotiations between the warring parties with a wish to achieve an objective. What's important is that Colonel Marticic didn't say that civilians would be targeted. The Prosecution in paragraphs 165 to 222 of its final brief, the Prosecution is also relying on and also in the introductory part of its closing argument, the Prosecution would like the Trial Chamber to believe that there is an alleged confession of General Galic that civilians were deliberately targeted, and that there were threats that existed and that they could be grounds for concluding that such attacks existed. Now, we would like to remind -- to look at the testimony of Henneberry, Razek, Mole, and also the witness -- another witness who was testifying during private session. I do not wish to utter his initials. I would like to ask you if we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's confirmed on my screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we are speaking about the threats, and this is in paragraph 183 of the final Prosecution brief, that the -- General Galic allegedly addressed to Witness Razek, and this is one claim that Prosecution makes that General Galic had confessed and that is regarding the testimony of General Razek, who said that -- what was said is that the other side continues to shoot at his units or against his units. He will continue to attack them. I will make them live difficult times. This is allegedly what General Galic told General Razek. The Defence would like to state here that this is regarding the legitimate target by military action which will be undertaken against the forces that are attacking his army, his troops. In such a threat as allegedly General Razek heard, that was addressed to the Muslim army, civilians are not mentioned at all. Also, we would like to stress that the threats that were allegedly made by a general superior to General Galic were not addressed to civilians. The fact that one tram had been hit, in the Defence's opinion, cannot be understood to mean -- to designate deliberate targeting civilians in tramways. The testimony of Witnesses Ashton and Henneberry regarding the contents of their discussions with Major Indic were counted by the testimony of Witness Indic who told us after what the Prosecutor told him what Witnesses Ashton and Henneberry told him, he said this was all lies. So what the Prosecution says that there is evidence regarding the confession of General Galic and his superior, his superiors and subordinates, that they deliberately targeted civilians, this has not been proven. Such allegedly -- alleged claims that the witnesses made, they cannot be understood to be a confession. Bearing in mind the testimony of all the witnesses, as well as UN observers and UNPROFOR members, the Defence believes that General Galic was a real officer and that such words or threats he certainly would not have addressed to anyone because this is something that he finds alien as a man and as an officer. The Defence, before allowing my co-counsel to continue, the Defence would like to give its view on the sentence. In paragraph 778 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution suggests that the degree of criminal responsibility, if General Galic would be convicted, should be such that it takes into account the number of wounded and killed civilians as well as the number of direct victims of the campaign and the psychological sufferings inflicted upon them as a result of the terror, and the physical effects that this campaign had, that such acts had on the ordinary course of the victims of the civilians during the relevant period, in the ordinary course of their life. The Prosecution has not proved their position about the significant number of victims in their suggestions. We claim that it is false to claim, as the Prosecution says, that General Galic supported the campaign. Everything points to the fact that General Galic respected the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, that he forbade civilians to be taken as targets, and there is no evidence that would prove that he implemented any sort of a campaign which targeted civilians. The claim the Prosecution made in paragraph 781 is also incorrect, the claim according to which these were continued crimes about which General Galic received daily information of the number of victims ran into the hundreds of thousands, the number of victims as a result of terror. And we think -- it is our opinion that the number of victims was far lower given the urban context of the conflict if compared to the victims in other battlefields that one has witnessed in the course of the history. When the Prosecution requires that a term of life imprisonment be met out, we think that the Prosecution hasn't seriously analysed the events concerning Sarajevo. They neglected the facts presented according to which the Muslims provoked and carried out attacks. That very fact would be sufficient to consider that the criminal responsibility -- the degree of criminal responsibility of General Galic, if he should be considered to be criminally responsible, responsibility at all, this degree should be considered to be the minimum degree in terms of his command responsibility within the hierarchy. Therefore, in the opinion of the Defence, a sentence could be given to General Galic only if one faced the difference between objective and individual responsibility as prescribed in the statute. And only if one considered that General Galic was objectively responsible in his capacity as corps commander, because no other form of criminal and legal responsibility, whether according to the provisions of Article 7(1) and 7(3) -- according to both these provisions of the Statute -- according to both these Articles, his responsibility has not been proven. So the Defence stands by its position that General Galic should be declared innocent on all counts in the indictment. The Defence also wanted to turn very briefly to the Prosecution's introductory remarks with regard to sniping incidents, although we would like to point out that the Defence has analysed these items in detail in its final trial brief. And given the restrictions of time, I have already pointed out that my colleague, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, shall continue with his presentation of this oral final trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

More precise than it was yesterday, although my guess was quite close to what Madam Registrar tells me, that is up until yesterday, the Defence took two hours and 30 minutes, so at this very moment, it's two hours and 50 minutes spent by the Defence. That means that there's remaining two hours and 10 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. First of all, I would like to greet everyone present here in the courtroom, and I apologise because my delivery will undoubtedly be somewhat different than usual, and the tone of my voice will certainly be a little different. So perhaps I will ask you to allow me to have a pause, to go and take a little medicine outside. Having said that, Mr. President, what I wanted to say first of all concerns figures. And since we are talking about figures, we will start first of all with Mrs. Tabeau. I would like to tell the registrar first of all who has helped us in an admirable way throughout these proceedings, I would like to ask Madam Registrar to prepare the Tabeau report, and we will show - not right now but in a minute - page A416, page 98. I have already made a copy to facilitate the task for you. Obviously, if you want the original, I'll understand that. But we have copies available if necessary. This document should be placed on the ELMO to enable everyone to see it. Mr. President, figures are figures. And the first thing that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we'll be struck by the figures when we take into consideration the brief of the Prosecution. In fact, nothing, almost nothing, is said about the so-called Tabeau report, the expert report which nevertheless comes directly from the Prosecution. But from the very beginning of its case, the Prosecution did not cease to say that they wanted to demonstrate mathematically by using figures, they wanted to prove the reality of the facts that they alleged. And in these initial documents in the indictment and in all its briefs that follow the indictment. Very well, Mr. President, Your Honours, what is the reality that we are speaking of? We will have ample opportunity to return to the figures in the Tabeau report. But the first thing that we have to point out is that the Prosecution never turns -- almost never turns to these -- to its own figures, and for an obvious reason. And we want to show that their own figures prove the contrary of what the Prosecution wanted to prove. Just one example in order to provide a framework for the hearing, this concerns the existence or the lack of existence proven by the figures. One should remind everyone, everyone knows this, "afirmanti non incubit probatio." And is it incumbent upon the Prosecution to prove this, not to the Defence. And its a contradiction, and not the only one, to see that it is the Defence that is going to provide this proof. On the 24th of July, table 3 and 4 in the Tabeau report, these figures haven't been accepted by the Defence. But since they come from the Prosecution, what better proof could one have than the proof that your enemy offers you. Very well, the figures are quite clear and almost transparent. For the initial period of the conflict, the first few months from April to September that don't concern the accused, that's a period during which the majority of the victims -- we had the majority of the victims. Do we have a problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked some pages to be put on the ELMO as far as I remember, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only asked for one page, Mr. President. I didn't ask for it to be placed on the ELMO. That's why, Mr. President. Is it --

utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, though, Mr. President, for your assistance. I'll carry on. I apologise. You'll see it in a minute. I'll inform you of when this will be necessary. Thank you. As the very figures prove -- [In English] It's not necessary to have it now. Thank you so much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was my mistake, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll carry on. These figures, Mr. President, Your Honours, prove that during the first five months, from April to September 1992 - 1992, as one says - we have something -- we have 7.085 wounded. That's about 1.400 wounded a month. And as against the successive periods, 12.900 would be the figure. That would be for the 23 months of the indictment. We would have 560 cases more or less. So if you have a look at the figures, one can see that during the period during which General Galic was in command, there were a lot of victims [as interpreted]. The proportion of victims was quite great. My question is as follows: For someone who has been accused of having amplified a campaign, shouldn't one admit that the figures are really strangely in his favour? The truth is that these figures prove that since General Galic assumed command, the number of victims obviously to a large extent diminished, and it is quite certain that there still were victims. But the Defence claims, and we will prove this, that to the extent that one can admit this and unfortunately to something that we have to admit, these figures are to a large extent as the result of circumstances of war conducted in a theatre of war which is an urban theatre of war, and I would like to underline this. It occurred in surroundings where it is almost impossible to avoid what one calls in technical terms scientifically collateral damage. These figures prove other exculpatory matters. One of the first things that the Defence has always pointed out concerns snipers. What is a sniper? The Prosecution's case is to say anyone bearing infantry weapons, anyone who can fire, who can hit a victim, whether it's the sower of death or a simple soldier's rifle, this doesn't matter. The result is the same; you have someone who is killed or wounded. That is a sniper. But in Tabeau's report, there is an internal contradiction which we can't resolve. When we have a look at the tables, you see the mention of the word "shelling" and then also the word "sniping," and then you have other firearms and other categories. And our question is: Why make a different categorisation? Why do you have sniping on the one side and other firearms on the other hand if we shouldn't do that and put it all into the same basket? Because when you have a look at these figures and you see 253 snipers, I wouldn't say only with regard to other things, but I don't want to be misunderstood if I say "only," this should be taken in relative terms. 253 sniping cases, and about 100, 101, 102 other arms. It doesn't matter. As long as we don't know what the methodology is used to distinguish snipers in the strict sense from other arms, what can show in terms of evidence, in terms of the presumption of evidence -- presumption of innocence that we shall all respect here? How is one to know that one is is not mistaken and that there weren't 253 cases of other arms and a hundred cases of sniper arms? This is a pure hypothesis. But how can it be proved that I should reject this? These are the documents that are the origin -- that come from the Prosecution and not from the Defence, never from the Defence. So why mention these other firearms if it was never necessary allegedly to do so? As the Prosecution says nothing about this, my question is: Why such silence, such persistent silence on the part of the Prosecution? If not because that is one of the areas, and that is where the problem appears or where things aren't resolved for the Prosecution. I see, Mr. President, that I should be listening to another channel because contrary to my habit, well now I can check -- I can verify what is happening elsewhere. As far as justice is concerned, Mr. President, the question is quite simple. If this distinction was made by the Prosecution itself, how am I to explain the methodological procedure, the methodological basis for this distinction was not really even presented by the Prosecution? There is something that is illogical, completely illogical there. And the Defence, to the extent that this is possible, is going to attempt and hopes that it will succeed in constructing its final examination of these facts and developing its final examination on the basis of only two items. On the one hand, on the basis of logic; and on the other hand, on the basis of common sense and truth. To this effect, the Defence has provided elements as mentioned that are quite disturbing with regard to sniping cases. The Defence has drawn the attention of everyone and of the Trial Chamber to the number far too great of these documents of a medical nature where when faced with a sniping incident or other incidents, I don't know how I should describe them, we can see the word "unknown." The site "unknown." My question is as follows: Can one logically admit, even if the situation concerned is a wartime situation, and we can imagine how difficult it would be and how traumatising at moments to work in such a situation, how can we explain that so many cases of wounded people, dead people, are referred to as having occurred in unknown places? I'm trying to imagine a body, a lifeless body, and of course somebody has to take it somewhere, take it somewhere, perhaps a mortuary. How can a person not know where they found that dead person? Imagine a wounded, an injured person. If that person is going to the hospital, that person knows where he had been hit, and if he's not going by himself, then he was driven there and driven by somebody. If that somebody -- wouldn't that somebody know where he had assisted this wounded? So now so many unknowns, so many unknowns. Of course, so many unknown female persons. For the English booth, for the English booth, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. unknown. For the Defence, the answer is clear, is that the facts were not disclosed. They could not be disclosed. They could not be ignored. On this point, the Defence believes that they have proven an important fact. This is the existence of certain manipulation which begins with figures and that we would like to see concluded with a set conviction. But this is the same manipulation -- I apologise for using this term. We're speaking of the same universe. And regarding this matter, the Defence would like to stress this is not a coincidence that although the Prosecution did have the means, refused to present the victims by clearly indicating geographically locations of incidents, although they could have done it. What about if this map, Mr. President, what if this map had allowed us to see how close or much closer these locations could have been to the front lines than we would imagine? I think this could have been done for all the 150 incidents. So this, for the Defence, would have been very important to demonstrate the reality of collateral damages, of stray bullets, of ricochets. Why they didn't do this? We could see that Prosecution was extremely competent to produce technical items, maps with details, photographs that allow us to see the world around us, everything in this courtroom. But this simple calculation, why not having done it for me? I'm asking this question. I'm asking these questions that nobody can answer. Now, let's look at the thesis of the Prosecution, and particularly regarding the sower of death. One of the main thesis of the Prosecution is to say that Serbs were barbarians, that's not what they actually said but it is to this effect. They were such barbarians that they were using a horrifying engine, machine, device that they were able to terrorise the people. So terrorised by it, they called it the sower of death. We know that that is an M84, and we have heard testimonies. And of course, sometimes some peculiar witnesses, but we heard that Serb held high points, that they had these sowers of death, that they were extremely accurate, extremely rapid, that they were causing great damage, that they had a huge force of impact, that they had binoculars, at any moment they were able to see anybody, child, woman, old person, target them, and open fire. And -- but I have the figures of the Prosecution. And I would like to ask you to look at A38 table and A39 of the Tabeau report. We can look at the column 84, that is, M84 column, the famous sower of death and the like, says the text, and look at the number of civilian victims. But before that, let's look at the overall number of victims that was caused by the sower of death. 11 victims. That is almost on my two hands, almost on my two hands. So on one side, there are nine men; and on the other side, two women. But if I look at civilian populations, I can also do it on my two hands, but I have to do it with my fist clenched. In the clear figures of the Prosecution, there isn't a single civilian victim that would have been caused that was produced in tables A38, A39, victim that would have been caused by the famous sower of death. This is what the evidence of the Prosecution showed, so these are barbarians, these Serbs who were targeting from the hills around the city, they never caused a civilian victim. Thanks to the Prosecution figures, the Defence has proven that if the Serbs had had these weapons and if they were able to see the city and the civilian inhabitants, and if they had the ability to destroy them. Now if they haven't done that, that means that they respected two things: Conventions and, more specifically, the famous principle of distinction. Now, what I wish to say here, Mr. President, and I spoke about manipulation earlier, and I'm going to say it because I believe that in Sarajevo, they used to be Emil Zolja Street, but there were also Zoljas, that's true, but there was Emil Zolja Street, and as Emil Zolja said, what we wish to say is: "I accuse," referring to the manifesto. I accuse. We cannot, when we look at the figures that have their own truth, and when we are looking at one's own figures, we cannot come and claim the opposite of what the figures show. You said, Mr. Ierace, that the closing argument has to be based on the elements, and that is what the Defence is trying to do, to confirm through the testimonies that the Serbs would have killed civilians by their weapons. But when we look at the figures that are showing the contrary, that is to say the at least surprising. In other words, Mr. President and Your Honours, how as part of the campaign, and I am saying the word "campaign," can you imagine a single instance of this situation, and the answer to this question, the Defence believes that this is simple logic which is self-imposing. It is so self-evident that if the Serbs had been in a position to do it and if they did not do it, it's because, and this includes General Galic, they did not wish to do this. Mr. President, I now would like to go on to another subject. We will come back to Tabeau figures. But let's look at the contradictions. One of the first contradictions is that we had two briefs of the Prosecution, one electronic and one hard copy. And I was only able to work on the electronic version. I've already informed, but I'm informing the registrar now, and in order to proceed logically and to see the Prosecution prepared its brief, is that I am going through the numbering which is a little confusing. I will cite the number that I have, the number of the page, and also the number at the end of the page which is right next to this number, of the footnote, so I hope that we will be able to find our bearings among these three elements. It will be a little longer, but again, the Defence is trying to be logical with the elements that it was given. As a part of the time that we were given, we cannot look at all of the contradictions that are included in the brief of the Prosecution, but we can only look at some of the most important ones. One of the first contradictions that struck us was that the -- this case, and I'm not only speaking about the brief but the Prosecution's case can be characterised by an absence. There is something missing in this case, and that is proof. There is something that is missing. There is a missing factor, and that is proof. There isn't a single document that could establish the beginning of proof. English booth, that's not quite what I said, but it doesn't matter. There is not even a shadow of the proof --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... As far as the translation is concerned, would you please address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Of course, Mr. President. There isn't a single document, single document that would demonstrate the reality of a written proof, a written order, illicit order given by General Galic to any of his subordinates. The position of the Prosecution on this point is very particular. They say they want a life sentence, not because they have proved, they have given such and such an element as it was the case in other trials here that we know very well. But knowing that this would be proven, why is that? And this missing factor, regarding this missing factor, the Prosecution said that they were not able to have all the elements of proof. Very well. But what does that mean? How come that the other elements that they don't have, how come they wouldn't have proved the innocence of General Galic, but they would have proven his guilt? We can see that there is no logic here. And that is the reason why the Prosecution has founded everything on the famous document of the 14th of May, 1992, document that was submitted as part of the Donia report. It is the only written document, the sole written document regarding which the Prosecution refer to. But the Prosecution keeps forgetting a detail. A tiny detail, three times nothing, and it's very important. From the very start of the war, the position of the man that you're judging today at the time he was Colonel Galic, he was not a general yet. Now, he did not say, "Destroy Sarajevo"; he did not say, "Eliminate all inhabitants"; he did not say, "Open fire," but "Defend without war." The text is very clear in Serbian; "bez da ret," without war. This is never referred to in favour of General Galic. Again, this is silence, which is inexplicable and unexplained. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, the exhibit that is in the Prosecution case, the Prosecution will try to found its case on something else. On the testimony of Mr. Henneberry, he is usually called "Young Captain Henneberry." And the Prosecution relied heavily on this testimony. And this witness would have been the only one to assist them in their case. And so, the Prosecution has done a peculiar thing. In order to support this thesis, they will, in extremis, by using another witness, that is Witness Cutler, here before this Trial Chamber, they will produce a phenomenon that is never seen anywhere, it is very peculiar, it demands to be mentioned, and this is a spontaneous regeneration of memory. After some ten years, ten years from when the events happened, we can see then suddenly a witness appears, suddenly, spontaneously. Although he had been questioned by the Prosecution for a long time, suddenly Henneberry, at the time Captain, now Major, they had never thought it useful at the time to inform his superiors or to leave any kind of written trace ever regarding this. And suddenly, here is this witness that arrives, a kind of Phoenix of evidence, he comes, he recovers his memory. And of course, he has very good reason, as you are able to see, this witness had the opportunity, had the opportunity, he had, in spite of the Victims and Witness Unit and all the restrictions, he was able to discuss all kinds of things with the other witness, the other witness being Henneberry. How can we believe particularly in The Hague that they were able to speak about good weather and nothing else? Although they were staying at the same hotel and that they were recalling -- they were walking up memory lane. So these two testimonies were so corrupted by this mechanism that they have no credibility. There is no quarantine for the witnesses who go over these restrictions, and they should be excluded. And now, stricto senso, I will now go to the brief of the Prosecution, that is, 64, page 23, electronic page, and the footnote nearby is 86. The Prosecution quotes General Rose to indicate that the total exclusion zone would have allowed the Serbs to redeploy their weapons. And I'm quoting here, I will do it in the language of the transcript. "To redeploy the forces to other places such as Bihac where they were able to intensify the fighting.." Transcript page 10.265. So why? What is the reason to mention these facts if we suppose it was proven, because no one charges General Galic with anyone concerning Bihac Gorazde. Why not mention Srebrenica and other places, too? If not to create confusion in people's minds, and to say if you want to be in Sarajevo -- perhaps if you want to be good in Sarajevo, okay. If you want to be bad in Bihac, let's punish you because perhaps you were a bad general in Bihac or elsewhere. In other words, this confusion is not acceptable at this level. Cases must be dealt with by specialists. There must not be any corruption of the case, no confusion. To affirm this shows how little one pays attention to the rules that we should all pay attention to, the rules that should dominate our work. And likewise for point 67 that follows. The Prosecution will say, okay, the anti-sniping agreement, you didn't sign it. We take note of that. But the Prosecution forgets, and they should be aware of this fact, the person who prepared that agreement, the person who made it possible to be established is General Galic. Why forget this fact? And its truth has been established. 66, 24, 61, another contradiction. It's one of these impossible equations without a possible solution as suggested by the Prosecution. The campaign Sovo Losa [phoen] campaign, was its objective to destroy the morale of the combatants by reminding them that while they were fighting, their families were in greater danger than they were themselves. And that same affirmation appears in page 80, 29. Mr. President, the same exercise, the same logic, the same truth. The figures produced by the Prosecution, and I'm referring to Tabeau. These figures show the following, and I'll quote the report in English: "The vast majority of those killed or wounded were men, 3.374 killed. Most of them were of active military age, 18, 16, 69 years, and were soldiers." Tabeau, 5, and there are figures to support it. And our question is as follows: What is this campaign directed against civilians that is going to produce, and I will quote the Prosecution -- that is going to result in mainly military losses where the victims were mostly men of fighting age, not women and children, and the victims were not only men who were of an age to fight; they were soldiers, too. And for once, I'm in agreement with the Prosecution when they say that logic should govern our discourse. And this can only mean one thing, Mr. President: First of all, if in the -- if the majority of victims were soldiers, people -- men who were of an age to fight, and this is quite obvious, that's why they were targeted, that's quite obvious. So how can I -- how can the victims be men who are of an age to fight if I am targeting civilians? And secondly, the minority, that is to say, other parts of the population were not targeted on a major scale. That's also logical. And the third logical matter I want to mention, this vast minority, although they were far more numerous as far as the terms are concerned, with respect to the soldiers in Sarajevo weren't in greater danger. They were not in such a great danger, and this syllogism, Your Honours, is followed by a fourth issue. We have always followed logic, and we have always put things in perspective. It's well known that in modern wars, it is usually civilians who suffer the most. In Sarajevo, the case was reversed. But we know that civilians don't have the same means to protect themselves as the soldiers who have bunkers, flak jackets, helmets, weapons, et cetera, experience. In order to be able to inflict casualties among soldiers, it's necessary to fire more often than it would be necessary if you were firing against people who are not soldiers. I am talking about the possibility of firing areas. This is to say that these figures must be put in perspective. They must be in favour of the General, of the accused. If a shell falls in a civilian zone, it will necessarily -- there will necessarily be civilian victims. I'm talking about collateral damage. If the shell hits soldiers who are protected, it is not necessarily that there will be victims, at least not the same number of victims. You need to use perhaps ten times more shells when firing at soldiers; if they are protected, perhaps 20 times that number of shells in order to obtain the same results. Yet again, this shows that in order to cause such a large number of military victims, then the vast majority of shots would have to be directed against the soldiers and not against civilians. That is quite obvious. This obvious fact has to be underlined once again. It's simply mathematics. One should point out that there's one soldier for eight civilians within the PAPA zone. That was the ratio of soldiers to civilians which was present in the so-called PAPA Sarajevo zone. So if we have, and this is obviously according to the Prosecution itself, the vast majority of civilians who have not been affected, who have not been hit, and we have this vast majority of soldiers in a situation where they are in the minority and the relation is 1 to 8, the figures speak for themselves. They are even more clear. Mr. President, the efforts one has made in this case to affirm things that are not true, and my question is: Why was it necessary to arm-wrestle in order to arrive at what one might consider truth? And why not see the reality of the figures? Why not want to discuss them, whereas they were provided to us? The Defence has had the opportunity of saying this. You can't kill the truth. You can stifle it, but one day or another, the truth will out. One day, it will be necessary to accept that there were, for example, campaigns, real campaigns in Dresden, 40.000 dead in three or four days. The Defence has said this. The Defence has also referred to Swinmund, 20.000 dead in a few hours. And the Defence would now like to ask, can these things be compared? Can this be prepared to the 253 sniping cases referred to by the Prosecution that have not been proven? With regard to these 253 sniping cases that have not been proven, the Prosecution wanted to establish the existence of a campaign -- of a campaign to terrorise the civilian population. The Defence claims that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they are very far from having proven this. But if one really examines the figures, matters, the debate would have been a lot clearer and truth would have been determined for the sake of justice. And another contradiction, I'll mention page 17, 26, 99, the Prosecution in order to better support its position tells us the following: In fact, why target the interior of the city since everything happened at the lines, and the fact that you targeted the interior of the town meant that you wanted to hit it and have victims and to inflict terror. And the Prosecution claims that operations were never conducted from the rear. How can one imagine such a thing in reality? And then there are witnesses, Prosecution witnesses who appeared here and proved the contrary. There was Mr. Kapetanovic himself. 79, 58, he must know what was at stake, he was one of the victims, and he knows General Briquemont. And not only the last witness that I mentioned later on in another context, not only did he confirm that attacks were carried out from the city, but he also said that it was inevitable, that this was inevitable when operations were ongoing, it was inevitable to have shells falling on the city. 10.131, he said the following: "It became inevitable," and he added for the period he was acquainted with where the Prosecution said General Galic allegedly targeted the city in retaliation, and I will quote what he said in English. [In English] "The shelling in December was shelling between two armies which were trying to destroy one -- to destroy military targets essentially." [Interpretation] Same page as before. And we are referring to the part of the town that was under Muslim control. And this proves several matters. Operations were conducted from the city. It was inevitable to have shells hitting the civilian zone. And the shelling was of a military nature. It is also true that this witness confirmed that the Serbs and the Croats in July accepted certain agreements, certain peace agreements. But those who refused were the Muslims, the enemy side. 10.045, page 30, after the footnote, 1, 2, 3, at 85 and 92 as well, the Prosecution claimed that the accused should never apparently, allegedly conducted investigations and that the Defence didn't provide any pieces showing the contrary. Mr. President, I don't know how to describe that. It is not because of a lack of an imagination, it is perhaps as a matter of courtesy, because the Defence has proven this by providing documents -- we refer to documents where one sees very clearly - they were provided by expert Radinovic - we see very clearly that such instructions, such orders to carry out investigations were given. They were provided within the chain of command, not only from a general to his subordinates, have a look at who opened fire, what they targeted, what the circumstances were. This was reported. But in other cases also it was said that no one should leave the area. Why these investigations? And then there were also reports from the superior command to General Galic, and General Galic reporting to him. It was stated that it wasn't possible to take action immediately but that there would be an answer in the following hours. So I will talk about these documents later on. So to affirm that not a single document was provided, it's a little, how should I put it, surprising. The question then is to know why? Why is one attempting to affirm this given that not only did the witness say that this was done, but the documents in the case prove this. We have already said, let's see who benefits by the crime. 86, 31, and before, 124. Mr. President, Your Honours, there is something almost moving for the Prosecution given that one wants to continue affirming that the accused was involved in a campaign, whereas all the figures prove the opposite. And wouldn't it be more in conformity with professional ethics, this is the question that I'm asking, wouldn't it be better to admit the simple reality, the fact that the number of victims didn't cease to diminish when General Galic assumed command? Furthermore, there is a calculation, and this is something that struck me a little later perhaps, but better late than never, there is a calculation that the Prosecution never did. What was the proportion of victims, of civilian victims, reported to the soldiers from April to September 1992? That is to say, during the months that preceded General Galic's command? What sort of light could we shed on this? 67, 60, 271. And this is what the Prosecution claims here. If the accused himself complained, and I'll quote: "Repeatedly - the word repeatedly - about such attacks carried out against the Serbs" - and we're talking about sniping fire, Muslim sniping fire directed at the Serbs, and this has been accepted by the Prosecution, this shows that the accused would have been aware that such attacks were illegal. And thus, those committed by the Serbs would also be of that nature. One should not go too far and put the ass before the cart. The first question. If that's the case, and the Prosecution claims that it has been proven, that there were such illicit attacks directed against Serbian civilians, attacks launched by Croat or Muslim forces, and this happened frequently because of the complaints, and if nothing distinguishes these attacks from the alleged Serbian attacks, then why does the Prosecution -- why didn't the Prosecution do anything in this respect against the Muslim or Croat forces. At school, Mr. President, I was always taught - these are old memories for all of us - I was always taught that one should add up the apples to the apples and the pears to the pears and not to mix things up; the situation is the same. Why do we have a different manner of treating these matters? Isn't this the proof - this is what the Defence claims - that the attacks on the one side, on the Muslim side allegedly against the Serbian side were not violations of international humanitarian law, but if they can be compared to the Serbian attacks, then the Prosecution has proven that the other attack which is comparable are not violations either. I don't see at all logically speaking what other conclusion we can have, particularly since the Prosecution officially admitted that the barriers that were set up in the Serb zone in Grbavica were established and set up in order to protect the civilians from the incoming fire. And speaking about the snipers. And that is not the most peculiar thing. The only thing that was proven regarding the sniping and the incoming fire is what happened in the Serb area. The Prosecution officially formally admitted that there were barriers in the Serb zones in order to protect the Serb civilians from incoming fire, fire coming from the Muslim area. So this is rather peculiar to see when we know the strictness of the Anglosaxon system that we are trying to apply here. The fact proved, when the other facts are not proven, and then other consequences are drawn. And regarding this matter, Mr. President, to see the problem of Serb victims on the Serb side, behind Serb lines, and the argument is not going to work either. What they will say, there is just one or two Serbs who died, so that's not important. But first of all, the Prosecution never tried to find out how many civilian Serb victims died on the other side. And that would have been very important. Secondly, the Defence proved that there were P16, P17, that the civilian Serb victims through their -- regarding their numbers were more significant than other casualties. Again, the silence on the side of the Prosecution. Ilidza destroyed, shelled; Nedzarici, shelled, destroyed. Serb parts of town -- Serb parts of Sarajevo, wouldn't they have to be looked at by history and by your judgement in the same way that the Muslims parts of Sarajevo would have been looked at, like Stari Grad, that were less destroyed. Does it mean that us lawyers, to follow up, to continue with false truths just like the propaganda people did, should we follow suit? Personally, Mr. President, I do not agree. That was civil war that was conducted in a terrible surroundings. But at the same time, one has to be reminded, the majority of civilian victims, the majority of civilian victims were a minority compared to the overall figure. All of these victims were a minority; the large majority were military victims. One other tendentious point that the Defence would like to examine in the next five minutes before the break, it appears under 238, 420, 85. This is regarding General Karavelic's testimony. This is the corps commander of the BH army. And this is the man who was the key person, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he should know things. And the Prosecution never showed, never asked this witness specific questions regarding the front lines, and asked him to give statement regarding these front lines. And we all know, except for the Prosecution apparently, is that the memory of this witness, when we tried to unfold one of the maps, large maps, he looked at it, and he made a gesture and said, "This was designed by amateurs; this is not a good map." Now, why would anybody be asking questions of a witness regarding a map that he believed -- that he believed had been drawn up by amateurs? The Prosecution -- the Defence does not wish to deal with amateurs. And it is the same case, Mr. President, with the funerals. 415, 92, 1.092. We are speaking about DP1. Here we are, the ceremonies, Serb funeral ceremonies were not shelled. Otherwise, he would have told us. But two are things here: The first thing is that this person only was present at two funerals during the war. It's rather a low number to draw a general conclusion. And the second thing is this person told us that this cemetery in question was at the Kosevo Hospital cemetery -- the Kosevo park cemetery which was allegedly constantly shelled. Now, we can see that the proof becomes a kind of -- it's a snake which bites its tail. And it is true, if we look at the map very closely, we'll be able to see that there were no really Muslim cemeteries. That seems peculiar. But in the cemeteries, there were areas. There were Christian areas, orthodox, Catholic, Muslim, there were even partisan areas, those who were atheists. And they were buried there. So as such, there were no Muslim cemeteries, but just areas of cemeteries that were Muslim. But the Prosecution produced an exhibit 3625 regarding a shelling incident. If we look at the image that I saw yesterday, like we all looked at, what we can see is a tomb which is denoting a tomb of Muslim faith. But we can see the very same cemetery, in the same image, there are crosses. These are obviously Christian crosses. Cemeteries in Sarajevo, just like the population, they were a little mixed together, but the Prosecution did not wish to stress this too much. I will just finish another matter just before the break. 442 -- am I going too fast?

And to be more efficient, did General Galic give any orders to constitute even a single special unit in order to fire more effectively on the alleged civilian targets that they were targeting on the other side of the lines? The Prosecution doesn't allege this even. Did Galic even encourage in a speech or anything he said, did he encourage his troops in a speech to conduct themselves in such a criminal manner? Nothing has been demonstrated. Did he himself provide an example, specific example, by having an extremist attitude? There is nothing to say that he did. utterances.text: To conclude on this point, let's draw everyone's attention to the rules. The rules allow us to keep certain sources of information quiet. Why? As far as the alleged threats are concerned - my colleague spoke about these a minute ago - it's still necessary to prove that they were implemented. Who knows, it was perhaps just a manner of exaggerating a man who was nervous at the time and who says several times: "This happened to me. I said things I didn't really mean." I said I wouldn't make any comment of a brutal nature about these things. I never wanted to say anything by saying that, that I despised anyone. It's possible that for everyone to say things that that person does not mean. But it is still necessary to prove that the person wanted to kill. There is another thing that we have to say about the war, Mr. President. And unfortunately, this is what history bears on today. There is a war which took place not long ago. That's the war in Iraq. And if I refer to it, and we haven't been able to refer to it for chronological reasons, for obvious reasons, but I refer to it because it's an important example. In a few weeks of combat, and this has been accepted by the parties concerned, there were hundreds, perhaps thousands of civilian victims, dwellings destroyed, civilian vehicles were destroyed, hospitals, maternity wards were affected, were hit.
