utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Another problem is the figures on the other side of the line, and here that is the unknown for the Prosecution, DP17 and then DP16 proved the existence of important losses, important casualties. Simply, I would just like us to make a comparison between the figures given by DP17, approximately 300 civilians killed in that period in Ilidza with 460 soldiers killed, and 2.150 soldiers killed in Tabeau report. We can see the Tabeau report examines a part regarding Ilidza, entitled Ilidza, and we can see that these figures are completely fully comparable with those that are offered by the Tabeau [as interpreted] report. Now, if we extrapolate, Mr. President, these figures given by one witness, the level of all the brigades, however empirical the system may be, we will come to the obvious conclusion that there were practically as many victims and casualties on the other side of the lines as there were inside the PAPA area -- the PAPA zone. Here, I'm referring to Section 5, table 1 of the Tabeau report. That's where we can find the figures that are comparable. On the other hand, we can see that the testimonies show us that the situation was comparable on the Serb side to the non-Serb side. On the subject, I would like to refer to other witnesses. For instance, Witness Lasic spoke to us about some 240 victims on page 13.763. And Witness DP1, on page 13.936, and it is this last witness who gives us this figure. Witness DP10, who confirmed that many shells hit civilian facilities, reference 14.340. Witness DP9. We also have Witness Vukovic, 14.637. Witness DP8, 14.771. And finally, Witness DP19, 16.413 who confirmed his only son died as he was going into his building, a civilian building. Finally, we should mention the testimony on page 17.769 of Witness DP17 who referred to 120-millimetre shell that landed near the Blazuj hospital killing immediately on the spot seven persons and wounding 33 out of whom 2 died of their injuries. This correlation of figures did seem to prove that on one side, like on the other side, there was no campaign. We know dami factum [phoen], and the Defence has replied, has responded errati factum. Let us speak about the incident in Vasa Miskin Street. It is an incident due to a clearly proven manipulation from a Serb population almost exclusively targeted in Sarajevo of streets with obstacles, journalists coming near, everything ready for an operation, and great difficulty for this place, the exact spot to be hit from the Serb positions. However, this attack was attributed to the Serb side from the press, and you know what we have to think about that. DP1, DP2 testimonies, they are very clear, and they establish the reality of this kind of operation. And the reality of this case, of this incident, is the untruthfulness. It's a setup. We wish to be very clear. We have to take the consequences regarding this reality, regarding the accused, and take the consequences of the law. The proof has not been presented. Therefore, we cannot condemn. Falsehood or lie was never the weapon of the just. The lie is just a mask of an imposter. We have no right as lawyers, as men of law, to trust -- follow the Prosecution's case who did not wish to see the reality of this setup. And they were trying to prove to such an extent that among the Prosecution witnesses, there was an important number of UN witnesses who came here to testify as Prosecution witnesses under oath that this was a common location among the -- it was a commonplace thing among the UN personnel in Sarajevo for the firing by the Muslim side against themselves in order to exploit the military and political and mediactic [phoen] situation. It's the peak of the state that should be targeted here, legal, political, military, those who have decided on this. And I have to admit that regarding this point of such firing, it is very surprising that the Defence did ask this question on several occasions: How can that happen? How can you consider these facts? How can you consider other facts that were proven, like the one regarding those civilians who were systematically forced, a large number of them, to dig trenches at the front line? How can you consider, and I have written this many times, and I have never received a response, an actual response. No comment in this case is not satisfactory. Justice must come out victorious of this case, and it will come out by resolving the riddles. Because justice is not an engine to condemn, to convict. If Nedzarici's Serb part of town and Ilidza's Serb part of town had been destroyed, Doboj, Vojnicko Polje, and if this is not a result of a criminal act, which is what the Prosecution is saying to us today, how can one logically the Dobrinja, Vojnicko Polje for their part would be that? We can see here that logic cannot explain away this, but what cannot explained by logic is in general what is not true. The Prosecution was not able to bring any proof, but there is -- this is done in a monumental way, and we can all agree there was no evidence. The Defence regrets that we were not able to organise transport to go to the site; otherwise, we would have been able to see many things. There is one other -- there is one other thing, Mr. President. It's an ancient text, but it is very modern. I will only quote two articles and only partially. It is a little hard, the first one, Article 1, I have to say here that this is a fundamental text which I literally have in the palm of my hand. I believe that this is a legal monument. "Men are born and remain free and equal." Article 2: "The objective of every political association and -- the objective of all political association is the consideration of natural laws and unrenounceable of man. These rights are liberty, property, the security, and the resistance to oppression. Declaration of the rights of man, fundamental text." Regarding General Galic, it is important to remember these two articles. Freedom and resistance to oppression, and this is what he has continued to plead. Proportionality and distinction, but I don't know how much time I have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll have another 27 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That will be perfect. Proportionality, regarding the question of proportionality and the respect thereof, it may appear, but only prima facie, and we how much prima facie is important in this case. There could be an appearance of difference regarding the difference between the incoming and the outgoing shots. However, there are several observations I'd like to make. We know that there is an incoming shot. And when it explodes and frequently, they do explode, it is a lot more easier to distinguish, and therefore enter into the logs, into the figures, rather than when it is outgoing from Sarajevo on to Serb lines. And that it would go somewhere within the 237 kilometres of the front line of 2.000 square metres of the area, since there was not enough personnel to check all this and to keep it all under control. That is first point. Second point, the noise. When a shell lands in the city, you can hear this noise, but you can hear it -- several people can hear it. And we know that the technique was to hear it and to report it. This is what was the method. And here we have had a confusion because several persons may have heard the same thing, and then recorded it several times. Third thing, the Lima provocation fire, whether they were mobile mortars or not. This method was proven. But what the Defence furthermore, and that was through the testimony of General Radinovic, which is the doctrine that he's teaching, that when a battery is firing at you, you should look -- you should try and destroy it militarily. In order to destroy a battery, you can't use just one shell. Figures were given when he was testifying. And from memory, I think he was speaking about 25 shells or more that was needed in order to try and achieve about a hundred per cent of destruction -- 50 per cent of destruction. And to achieve 100 per cent of the destruction, to eliminate it completely, how many shells would have to be fired? This was the task of an engaged commander, to try and find the military enemy objective. And this explains why this exists, this difference between the incoming and outgoing fire. Fourthly, if the response was not calibrated and measured Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. proportional to the incoming fire, then we would have found a situation on the ground that would be completely different. We would have found the entirety of the city, not just the area of the conflict, not just the confrontation zone stricto senso, but the entire city, all of the areas, the old town, those the most fragile, completely shelled, completely destroyed. Looking at those fragile houses, weak houses made of stone, and there we would have had a city razed to the ground. Now, is that the case of Sarajevo? And the answer is clear, no. Is it true that the Prosecution was never able to bring into this case one single element of a building, symbolic building, which was of symbolic nature, that during the incriminating period, the period of the indictment, would be connected to General Galic, that that building was destroyed? Those of us who were here for 16 months of the proceedings, can we give one single building that the Prosecution can tell us that was deliberately targeted? We were speaking of a matchbox. But this is one of the highest buildings. That is not a symbolic building. And it is certainly a location where -- that the enemy fire could reach, and this was to do with the superior floors of the building from where the Serb forces could have been targeted the best. Nothing else. There were two facilities that the Prosecution mentioned. The famous national library, and the PTT building. But these two facilities, they were also hit outside of the indictment or the relevant period, and one of them could have been, according to what we call the dual use, a legitimate target, a legitimate military facility. And I think that this absence of documents, of these facilities, they would have been symbolic. That is another proof that the Prosecution brings. And there are others. There is a witness - I won't quote him because I don't know whether it was said in open or closed session - there was a witness who said on one Sarajevan hospital was a bullet pockmarked -- not bullets, it was shelled. It was hit by artillery, probably by tank fire. It had a crater that could have only come from the internal area, Muslim side, because there was a hill between the Sarajevo -- between the Serb forces and the hospital in question. The proof brought by the Prosecution, it was that the Muslim forces that managed to do this, and that is to fire at their own hospitals. Certainly, there is a state hospital, and I'll speak about Kosevo Hospital a little later, military hospital. So we have one witness, Witness Ashton. He tells us, state hospital, that was terrible. Every day, there was at least one artillery hit. But again, the Prosecution proves the contrary. When we listen to the doctor who worked there more than others, who had -- I will give his name. I think that it was in open session, Dr. Mendlovic. The greatest damage caused was the result of infantry fire, that is to say, the result of fire opened from normal firearms. He also says that the north side was less damaged, but it was damaged. And when we have a look at Mr. van Lynden's testimony, who was set up in his headquarters there, he says he only remembered one artillery shot, directed at this site. It is obvious that on the one hand, this fire -- not the artillery fire but the infantry fire, was the result of ongoing combat in the city at the time. It is also obvious that the testimony of Mr. Ashton was totally refuted by other Prosecution witnesses because how could one imagine that there was artillery fire every day directed at such a hospital, whereas those who lived there said the contrary, and those who were based there only mentioned one incident, one case of shelling. And Ashton is an odd journalist, yes, an odd journalist, because this witness, this freelance journalist, when he was wounded and apparently this is the sort of treatment that the press is very interested in, he was evacuated by the American forces. He was treated at an American base in Germany, and then treated at a hospital -- a private clinic in Germany if you please, and he never paid a cent for this. I know that journalists are people who lead interesting lives, but should not one think of what Mr. Indic said, that Ashton was a special agent who had been sent by certain American agencies in order to see what -- to have a better view of what was happening in Sarajevo. Hence his rather particular testimony. Let's remember that when the tank allegedly fired on a facility, he climbed up on the roof to take photographs as a journalist. He took his camera, but alas, he forget to some film with him. Very well. Very well. Whatever may be the case, the figures speak for themselves. And the figures from the Prosecution speak against the Prosecution and in favour of the Defence. If I shell on a daily basis and within the framework of a campaign, so many hospitals and so many occasions, there would have been a lot of victims. And that would have been known, that would have been established. There were certain medical personnel who were wounded. But we can count them on the fingers of our hands. And the Defence doesn't think that this could prove the existence of a campaign. I will now move on the subject of orders. Could we move into private session now. I would appreciate that, Mr. President, just for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with regard to that matter, well, how can we exclude three possibilities? First of all, the fact that a shot was a result of a soldier who was not obeying orders. You know that sometimes there are lawyers who don't obey. Why shouldn't there be soldiers who fail to obey, too, but who don't report this? Secondly, the shot was fired by someone who wasn't under the orders of General Galic, and I would include people from the Seva group. Thirdly, a certain wound wasn't the result of a certain shot but was result of an error. While I would appreciate it if one could show me how we could exclude these possibilities and on what basis. Just one example what the Prosecution could have done because we know that there are only 253 sniping cases, alleged sniping cases. Let's not examine 20 or 24, but with regard to these 253 cases, they could have given precise indications that would have allowed you to verify what the reality is. This was not done. And I have to repeat it very clearly [Latin phrase]. Thank you very much. And I know that with regard to this matter, the Prosecution would agree with us. The Prosecution could have done this, they could have presented these 253 sniping cases as proof, and 98 bis allows them to do this, and given that it would have represented nothing among the documents that we received, they didn't do it. They didn't prove it. They didn't want to prove it. They have to take this into account.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are using now and then Latin. As you know, Latin is not one of the official languages of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be a problem translating in English. So if you would repeat in French what you said in Latin, we are sure that the Prosecution also becomes aware of what you said, unless the Prosecution would now confirm immediately that they all are fluent in Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very sadly, Mr. President, I cannot confirm that I or my fellow lawyers are fluent in Latin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then ask you to repeat in French what you said in Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Latin phrase], the dice has been cast. What I have said, Mr. President, a minute ago is [Latin phrase], that is to say, it's not sufficient to have an -- alleged illicit acts unless there was an illicit intention present. It's not an illicit act unless there's an illicit intention. That's what I said, Mr. Ierace, and I was clearer in French. Have I been clearer in French than I am usually in Latin? I think so. The shelling incidents, Mr. President. No proof as to the origin of fire, of the alleged fire. And above all, I am no longer talking about the fingers of my -- of both my hands, but just about the fingers of one hand. Five incidents are concerned. Five incidents to prove the reality of a campaign during 24 months of a conflict. Five incidents for which we are told that the Serbs, nasty as they were, could have targeted all the bread queues, all the queues for humanitarian aid. And this happened almost on a weekly basis, and they knew where they were located because their information service was perfectly well organised. Five cases alone. Very well. The Prosecution claims that this -- that civilians were deliberately targeted in this shelling. That's not true. Let's take an example, very briefly, very rapidly. The football match. Why doesn't the Prosecution want to recognise the reality of the fact that the trenches were not 300 metres away as they said, but 50 metres away. That is what the situation was. Witnesses supported this claim. So it means ignoring testimonies and documents. It shows that there is the desire to convict General Galic and that the willingness to arrive at the truth does not exist. The same observations should be expressed with regard to Alipasino Polje. I have heard, and I was quite flabbergasted by this yesterday, the Prosecution said that the entrance of a building was targeted. But if the shot was fired from Nedzarici, the only thing that one knows is that in such contested hypothesis, the gunner would not have been able to see the entrance to the building. So how can we have such a setup, and what would the objective of such a setup be if not to prove that the Prosecution's objective is not to establish what the truth was, but to have recourse to the sort of [Latin phrase] in order to have General Galic convicted. Why not examine the possibility of an error? Let's examine the other incidents briefly. In general, we won't go into the details, because we have the documents that we are interested in. The Prosecution could have proved certain facts through the witness -- through its witness Kovac, an artillery expert. Very well. But this witness appeared here, and he claimed that these were all cases of murder. An artillery expert made this claim. And when the Defence intervened and wanted to cross-examine this witness to a certain extent to see what he really had to say, he was so disturbed that he no longer knew where he had met representatives of the Prosecution in The Hague. He no longer knew who Mr. Ierace was. So how can this be for an expert who comes here and says yes, those were murders, and no longer knows who gave him the mandate? We should have proceeded as in the case of Hinckley, the artillery expert who said on instructions by the Prosecution that he never saw a gunner. He said that as an expert, I affirm that these people did have the intention of firing above, or lower down, or to the left, to kill them or to wound them. What can that be? When one brings experts in order to prove the existence of mens rea, the intention, to say, yes, I wasn't there but I know very well that the person over there had the intention of doing what the person did, and these are claims made before here before this Trial Chamber. The Defence can never accept such claims regardless of decisions that your Trial Chamber might reach. As far as terror is concerned, this is a fairly -- this is a quite simple matter. Here we have a certain image. In order to seek the truth, an expert is provided with a photograph, an art collector, and he provides a piece of art and says confirm to me that this is -- for the English booth, he provides a photocopy of his painting, and he asks his expert "prove to me that this is an original." And this is exactly what the Prosecution did with Turner's report. Did one ask expert Turner to examine medical documents, to discuss with former patients? Did one even produce psychiatric documents, the records before, the records during the war, the records after the war, et cetera, et cetera, nothing was produced. And this expert witness wasn't even shown a plan of the town so that he might know where the legitimate combat zones were located along with the consequences that this implies. He was provided with a photocopy of the situation. He was said "stamp this, certify that this is original, there was terror," I'm asking you to do so, so do it. And that's it; end of case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, doing your calculations by hand now, it's five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm happy to see that you have understand me perfectly. And since I have only five minutes, these will my very last minutes. Markale. Markale. Markale. And the only thing I'll say in five minutes about Markale is that it was never possible to prove -- it has never been proven from which side of the lines these shots came. Anything else would be nothing but speculation, pure and simple speculation. The real battles, these are the battles conducted by experts. I have to admit that I am not an expert, not to the extent that Mr. Stamp is as far as algebra and mathematics are concerned. Sometimes I have difficulty in following these matters, so I will base myself on common sense and logic and we will see how in the case of Markale, there are far more troubling matters. There are a lot of matters that are disturbing. First of all, it has been proven in the case that there are 70, about 70 I didn't count the exact number, but about 70 shells exploding, 70 shrapnel pieces. 70 shrapnel pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I asked you to address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I apologise. About 70 pieces of shrapnel that were collected by the authorities in Sarajevo. These pieces of shrapnel, it has been proven that they were collected at the site immediately following the incident. And we are also told that, and such was the procedure, they verified that these were recent -- these were fresh shrapnel pieces, that's the term that was used, with regard to this incident. There is proof that these fragments were somewhere. It's in Document 60, Defence Document 60. We know that the visual analysis, mechanigraphical or chemical analysis could have allowed us to establish one matter: Whether these fragments were the fragments of one shell or not. In order to verify this matter, the Defence on several occasions requested the production of these pieces of shrapnel. We know that the MUP and the justice organs, the judiciary in Sarajevo possesses these pieces. At the very end of its case, the Prosecution told us: "Sorry we can't provide you with these pieces of shrapnel." End of story. And we cannot know since these fragments -- as far as these fragments are concerned, we can't know what the case might be. But what we do know is that they didn't want these fragments to be produced before this Tribunal so that might be in a position to analyse them. And the question was: What would have been the origin of these fragments? Did these fragments belong to one shell or to several shells? And by not allowing us to proceed in this manner, and I'm not referring to your Trial Chamber, Mr. President, I'm speaking in a very broad sense, but the rights of the Defence were violated for a simple and clear reason. If one had proven that these fragments weren't the fragments of just one shell, in that case, the Defence could have developed its case and could have clearly prove what it has always wanted to prove, namely, a certain lack of responsibility. The simple fact that these fragments were not produced has prevented us from doing this. But even more, the Prosecution goes further and proves the contrary of what they wanted to say. AK1 was an old witness whose hearing was perhaps not as good as ours but who was very clear and who said, Well, I heard a shell fly over my house, and he even described the sound of the shell. And we had a lot of witnesses and experts who said that you can't hear a shell that is not self-propelled. One can't hear such a shell in town. One could only hear such a shell under two -- in two conditions: If one is in immediate vicinity of the origin of fire, and one can hear it perhaps if one is there when the shell lands. In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your five minutes are over. I told you that we would be very strict. So would you please finish in one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, this witness proves that if he heard the shell, the shell could only have been fired from position -- the position where his house was located; that is to say, in territory it was not controlled by Serbian forces. And in one minute, the last point is probability. One talks about a debacle in Markale, but this was a very political debacle for the Serbs. Why would General Galic - and he's been described as an intelligent man to us - why would he have ordered his men to create such an a debacle given that we knew that this would have provoked the intervention of the international forces in Bosnia at the time. Therefore, this would have accelerated, if not provoked, first of all the end of the conflict; and secondly, would have resulted in the victory of his enemy. Why would this man who has been described as intelligent, why would he have desired such an effect, given that quite obviously this is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your time is over. I invited you to finish in one minute. You took that one minute. You have now 30 seconds and then it's over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say I am almost finished. I wanted to cite Tucker, who in response to one of your questions said, and I will quote in the language that he used, in English, [In English]: "To put it bluntly, the more suffering the better, because that plays to the television cameras and would ultimately lead to the pressure that they wanted in order to achieve international intervention." [Interpretation] 10.330, as -- 10.030, as in 30 seconds. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We'll now adjourn for 20 minutes. This also means that since the parties both have 30 minutes available. Looking at the clock, we'll start again at a quarter to 1.00. And since our time today goes until a quarter to 2.00, I expect the parties to keep well within the 30 minutes because the parties should finish by today. That also means that there's no time available any more to respond to any questions of the Judges, so therefore, the parties -- of course I do not know whether you'll use your full 30 minutes, but you should be prepared to continue tomorrow morning to answer any questions of the Judges still remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence had prepared to part immediately after this hearing, since we were granted this. But if we could have more time this afternoon, we would appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There will be no possibility this afternoon. We all were aware that we had a very strict order. And if everyone would keep strictly to the time that we might have finished today. But this was not possible. So I invite the parties to adapt their schemes to what is really, I would say, the last final part of the trial is very important. So therefore, I suggest that the parties would adapt their schemes. If there's anything to be said about this, we'll hear about it during the break. You'll give us the messages needed. We'll adjourn until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first like to deal with the order of this hearing. There will not be sufficient time available today for questions of the Judges. That means that at a quarter to 2.00, or perhaps a few minutes later, after the parties have finished their submissions, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 10:30, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you're looking at me. Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the break, I received no further information or further messages, so that's the decision of the Chamber. Mr. Ierace, are you ready to...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will start, and at a later point, I will hand over to Mr. Mundis who will respond to some of the submissions made yesterday on the law. I refer to the submissions in no particular order, and I will have to move fairly quickly in point form. In relation to the nonappearance of the fragments that were referred to by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we heard from Mr. Suljic that various departments in Sarajevo moved. And as a consequence, the fragments could not be located. And that clearly was the reason that the Prosecution was unable to produce them. Submissions were also made in relation to the statistical evidence presented by Ewa Tabeau. At the outset, the Prosecution did not set out to prove a particular quantification of civilian casualties as a result of the unlawful sniping and shelling; rather, the Prosecution took the view, as expressed in its pre-trial brief, that a minimum of 1.000 civilians were injured or killed as a result of the unlawful sniping and shelling. The evidence of Ewa Tabeau achieves that. The statistics go not only beyond 1.000, but they are seen to be conservatively obtained. The figures provided or referred to by Medecins Sans Frontieres accumulated after the survey which was the basis of the Tabeau indicated a much higher number. But it is ultimately of no consequence to the guilt or innocence of the accused as to what the final figure is. Mr. Piletta-Zanin referred to a table that indicated no deaths as a result of firing by the M84. And indeed, that is the case. And there's a very low figure in terms of civilian casualties, in the form of injured civilians, by that weapon. But of course, it goes without saying that survivors and injured victims themselves could not always be sure as to what type of weapon had resulted in injury or death. And the sniping category in that survey was not qualified in any specific way. Therefore, it is safe to assume that casualties attributed to sniping, for instance, do not relate necessarily to the use of just professional sniping rifles, but rather, various infantry weapons including the M84. Yesterday, Ms. Pilipovic referred to the evidence of Mr. Kupusovic in relation to his observations in the pre-indictment period, although not essential to the case against the accused, the Prosecution does stand by precisely what it said in its written submissions. And if one consults page 716 of the transcript, one will see there precise evidence by Mr. Kupusovic along the lines of what was in the written submissions. Yesterday and today, we've heard submissions in relation to another witness which requires me to go into private session briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the state hospital, the Defence said that van Lynden said it was only shelled once. That was incorrect. He did not. It then sought to isolate Ashton's evidence in relation to the state hospital suggesting that he was the only one who said that it was shelled on multiple occasions. That also is incorrect. One only has to look at the evidence of Dr. Nakas, the administrator of the hospital, and perhaps more significantly the evidence of Dr. Mendlovic who chose to stay on at the hospital. He could have left Sarajevo, Serbian ethnic background, but stayed on and worked throughout the indictment period. And he spoke eloquently about the constant shelling of the hospital. A number of individuals gave evidence about their direct observations of the upper levels of the hospital watching the flashes of muzzles on the SRK side of shells that impacted on the hospital or around it. We heard evidence that two of the witnesses actually were able to locate the source of the fire in terms of visiting the areas, van Lynden in relation to where he spoke with General Mladic, and Ashton in relation to positions he marked on one of his maps where he found the source of anti-aircraft fire that used to hit the hospital regularly admitted. Spahic, incident 9, the Defence says there was no shooting beforehand. Incorrect. She said that the reason they went out that day was because there was no shooting. Page 2.613. The Defence says why weren't bread queues targeted? Because everyone knew where they were, humanitarian aid handouts. Incorrect. The head of civil defence said that positions were charged for that very reason, so as to minimise the chance of bred queues being targeted. In any event, the objective according to the Prosecution was to terrorise, not to kill every civilian in Sarajevo. And that was achieved most successfully with indiscriminate shelling. A further observation in relation to Ewa Tabeau's statistics, to the extent there is a drop in civilian casualties, and that has been explained by a number of factors, essentially anti-shelling, anti-sniping techniques adopted not only by the UN and the local government authorities, but by the civilians themselves. For instance, children in particular being placed in basements. We heard from Medina Omerovic who spent an appalling 12 months living in a basement with many other families, one window, didn't save one of the other children in the basement, though. A 10 year old who was shot outside her apartment when he emerged from the basement. In relation to the correlation between military and civilian statistics when one looks at the graphs, that is, that civilian statistics would occur at about the same time as military statistics in terms of high points, one has to recollect the evidence that indiscriminate fire would be levelled at the city at the times of battles in order to bring pressure on the presidency, and that indiscriminate fire we heard resulted in civilian casualties. It cannot be assumed that it related to combat battle. That is not the evidence. We heard about Iraq and other battles. The principal distinction is this: This was not a hot conflict with the exception of occasional battles such as Zuc. This was a stalemate, and that is the evidence. That word has been used by witnesses to describe it. One would not expect from a stalemate situation the ratio and the figures that one obtains in a hot conflict such as Iraq and other conflicts. Symbolic targets, most of them had been destroyed by the time the accused took over. The post office, the library, the parliament building, the assembly hall. The Oslobodenje building was still standing; it had not been completely shelled. It collapsed shortly after the accused took over as a result of shelling in his period. Trams were very symbolic; they were attacked. The old city area to the east was constantly attacked through the accused's period. A highly symbolic area. The Defence acknowledged the symbolism involved in hitting the matchbox building. Mr. President, given the earlier intervention by the Defence, I'd be grateful for an indication of how much time we have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have still available seven minutes. And I deducted four minutes for the procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I hand over to Mr. Mundis, just briefly in relation to Richard Gray's evidence about the firing of the mortars that landed near the presidency. Everywhere that his evidence could be checked, either by reference to the video or the book by General McKenzie or other sources, he was wrong, and he acknowledged that. It was not possible to completely check him in relation to the source of the mortar fire, but even so, he acknowledged that he was the source of information for General McKenzie's account of that incident. He was the only UN person present. He reported to General Mackenzie. That was where General Mackenzie got his information. General Mackenzie did not say in his book that the shot emanated from the presidency side. He expressed some doubt about it. One infers directly from that that the view expressed by Richard Gray in the witness box was not what he told General Mackenzie. At that stage, he did not tell General Mackenzie that he heard the shot being fired from the presidency side. To that extent, we can check that. When one take into account those factors and his general lack of credibility, that is not a good example of fire coming from the Bosnian side. Thank you, Mr. President. I hand over to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, several issues concerning the law arose during the oral submissions of the Defence yesterday, and I'd like to briefly respond to just a few of them. First, with respect to Article 3 of the Statute, clearly if there's one legal issue that's settled in the jurisprudence of this tribunal, it is that Article 3 of the Statute is a residual clause covering any serious violation of humanitarian law, be it treaty-based or customary law entailing the individual criminal responsibility of the accused, the Tadic jurisdiction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down, please, when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Tadic jurisdictional decision settled that. With respect to cumulative charging, cumulative convictions which the Defence alluded to at pages 41 and 42 of yesterday's LiveNote testimony, again the Appeals Chamber has ruled on that and set forth a test that is applicable in that, and I will specifically point to the Jelisic appeals decision where the Appeals Chamber indicate had cumulative convictions for offences under Article 3 and Article 5 of the Statute are always permissible. Next, the Defence particularly with respect to the terror count undertook a textual analysis of the Prosecution's proposed elements of those offences. Clearly, the Prosecution in setting forth those proposed elements meant for them to be read together, that is, conjunctively in that all of those elements must be met. And for the Defence to argue that a threat is not necessarily unlawful in time of war, therefore, there was no terror, the Prosecution would submit is an improper reading of the proposed as we have set them forth in our brief. Let me turn very quickly to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to say that I'm urging the parties to finish as quickly as possible. So I feel a bit guilty for it. But I might grant one additional minute as I just did to the Defence as well. But if you could accommodate the interpreters, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the applicability of the additional protocols, and in particular, additional Protocol I, as is clear from Prosecution Exhibit 58, the 22 May, 1992, agreement between the parties, they agreed that notwithstanding the provisions of additional Protocol I and its general applicability with respect to international armed conflicts only, the parties specifically undertook an obligation to abide by the terms of specific provisions within additional Protocol I. Those provisions being set forth in that agreement and reiterated in the Prosecution's final trial brief. The Prosecution position is quite clear that those provisions were applicable on the basis of that special agreement. And in addition, of course, those provisions that are specifically relied or specifically set forth in that agreement, the Prosecution submits reflect customary international law nonetheless. And the fact that the parties agreed to abide by those provisions, notwithstanding the fact that it appears to be an internal armed conflict is of no consequence given the explicit agreement of the parties that they would abide by those provisions. Very quickly, with respect to the issue of proportionality, the Defence repeatedly stressed that this was a situation involving urban warfare, and that the civilian casualties were simply collateral damage. The Prosecution would respectfully submit that that is not the end of the analysis by any stretch of the imagination. This does not resolve the issue; the fact that it was an urban conflict does not relieve the accused or his subordinates of complying with the very specific provisions set forth particularly in Articles 49 through 52 of additional Protocol I and Article 57. Finally, the Defence raised the issue as to in effect charging policy of the Prosecution. That is, it's quite clear from the Tribunal's jurisprudence, is improper. I would cite to paragraph 180 of the Celebici decision in which case an accused unsuccessfully put forth a similar argument. The fact of the matter is the Prosecutor has discretion as to who she will bring charges against. The second part of that argument clearly goes to an issue which the Prosecution has repeatedly raised; namely, the improper use of a tu quoque defence. The Prosecution has submitted in its written brief at paragraph 710 through 718 a discussion of that issue. And the Prosecution will rely on its written submissions to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, your additional minute has started already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Finally, I think with respect to the issue of charging and discretion with the Prosecution has, Mr. Piletta-Zanin earlier today referred to history judging this institution for its failures to charge individuals that Mr. Piletta-Zanin thinks would be appropriate to be charged. Let me conclude by stating, Mr. President, that this tribunal will be judged in history not on the basis of any one individual case, but on the means by which the Prosecutor exercises her lawful discretion with respect to the totality of the cases which are brought before this tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Is the Defence ready? Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I did not respond earlier on the issue of the witness that was brought into question the nature of -- the status of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is confirmed to me by Madam Registrar that it was in open session. But you disagree still?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to sort this out, not at this very moment, at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If everything has been checked, if necessary, appropriate measures will be taken so that whatever may come to the public will come to the public. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I provided the registrar with the message a minute ago. She must have received it. I don't have the figures present at the moment. But one part was, and I wrote this down, one part was in closed session. That was the very first part. And everything else was in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as I told you, it will be sorted out, and the appropriate measures will be taken. Ms. Pilipovic, or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you ready to give your final --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we are ready. How much time do we have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For as long as -- for today. Can the time taken by the Prosecution, et cetera how much time do we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution took 30 minutes, and I granted one additional minute. I have a question for the booth. Would it be possible in order to finish the 30 minutes for the Defence by today that we would finish at half an hour from now on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, that's not a problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters, at least the English booth has confirmed that they will be willing to stay a little bit longer. So we can use this... So you've got 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but discussing this sometimes takes more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 30 minutes. To say the following: The Prosecution hasn't really replied to the essential matters. And it's not only that they haven't replied to the essential issues, but the Prosecution continues to follow the same route. It affirms, and yet again, I have to repeat, this is not acceptable. They affirm that we didn't produce documents to prove that the accused had had investigations carried out. These documents have the following numbers, with respect to the Radinovic expert report: D260, D245, D248, D255, and D254. And of course, Mr. President, this is the best-off presented to you by the Defence, but the best of also because the Prosecution doesn't want to recognise the reality of these documents, the existence of these documents. Why? Because they know that I will produce these documents. The Prosecution isn't completely unenlightened with regard to this. And they say, well, yes, Galic carried out investigations when he wanted to, as he thought was appropriate, and in a certain sense it was a pretext for other matters. Well, let's pause for five minutes and give thought to this at the time. This was a time of war. No one knows who is going to be victorious. No one knows who is going to lose the war. No one at the time thinks about the constitution of a tribunal such as this one? So why say these documents? Why say these documents, apparently the beginning of a coverup, of a masquerade? Thank you. And secondly, the Prosecution recognises, but barely, that not a single victim was produced by the sower of death. What they forgot to say was that they remained silent on this matter is that in its report, it says M84 and the like, and other machine-guns. So where are all these civilian victims, these civilian deaths, the civilians who were crossing the airport? And we were told that they were fired upon from machine-guns at night as they were crossing the airport. Where are all these victims? Well, the Prosecution has proven to me that they quite simply don't exist. So as we don't have that many civilians, we'll try and seek them among -- we'll try and seek out UN personnel, and we'll say if there aren't any civilians, they fired at UN personnel. Very well. The only evidence we have about this, the real evidence, is that we have alleged from General Morillon protesting about the Muslim party because they were targeted. We have the cassettes from the Seva group that says that one French soldier was killed by these Muslims forces although they wanted to protect civilians by the alleged barriers. Why discuss something that isn't at the centre of the debate. Why want yet again to concentrate on other matters in the debate given that we know the shots, that perhaps occurred on the Serb side were shots fired in response to fire coming from the surroundings of what we have termed the PTT building here, from which General Karavelic's forces operated. And on numerous occasions they were seen there. And that's where they perpetrated their acts. So isn't it easier to say, well, yes, you fired at the PTT building, or at other buildings, you fired on the peace forces, but the perspective should be a lot broader. It should be within the context of a general investigation, and this has nothing to do with the alleged civilian victims. Very well. The Prosecution took note of certain historical examples. They took note of the recent war, but that has nothing to do with it. The fact that these extremely precise modern weapons, no one in totally good faith ever said there was a US campaign to kill as many civilians as possible, to terrorise the civilian population in Baghdad or to empty the possessions of the museums in Baghdad. No one said that. But when we have such precise weapons that result in so many victims, why won't the Prosecution even discuss such consequences, the consequences of collateral damage. I have never heard the Prosecution address the matter of collateral damage on a single occasion. But he should examine things of an exculpatory nature after all. If we know that there was, and we know that the Prosecution has affirmed this, there was Muslim fire on the interior of the city, if we know this, we can admit that that is a possibility to have firing errors, in such case why would the Prosecution persist in saying that there were 253 sniping cases whereas on the other hand the Prosecution is aware of the fact that fire was opened that resulted in losses, and this fire did not have its origin from General Galic's troops. The origin of fire was in the interior. So does this indicate there was an intention, and it is not only logic that points to this intention, it's also the logic of justice and legal logic that points to these conclusions. As far as sniping rifles are concerned, we are told, it has been proven that they existed. Very well. First of all, we are -- they quote expert Radinovic, the Defence expert. But they forget to say that what was said at the time, and my colleague Ms. Pilipovic has mentioned this, Mr. Radinovic was speaking of the second half of 1994, and not of any other period, not of any other matter. But then we are told yes, but a witness saw rifles, and here at this point I would like to return to private session. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness D was a deserter. And how reliable can the words of a deserter be. Not only was he a deserter, but in addition, he was a mercenary in an army that wasn't his. He said that he was a Croat. And he was there for personal reasons, his personal benefit. It wasn't someone who was engaged because of under threat. He hadn't been forced to do so. He was there, he was paid, and he decided to engage himself. And he decided, well, this is bothering me, this is disturbing, I'll leave. That was the morality, that was the morality of this witness. But even if this witness may have seen snipers, wouldn't it possible that the sniper would be targeting legitimate targets on the other side? It doesn't mean that if I see a knife, it doesn't mean if I see a knife, someone's going to plunge this knife into the body of this person, and this is what the Prosecution has been doing. According to this witness, one doesn't even realise that this witness is also proving our positions. D says that he observed mortar shells being fired by people -- by men under the influence of alcohol. Very well. And he said "I felt bad." Very well. So I said he felt about this. Did you report these facts to your superior officers? Did you say "stop, I do not accept this morally as a man. I have to report this." And then this mercenary witness, this deserter, said: How can I report them because I was a Croat? Very well. Who believe -- who wishes to believe will believe. But affirming this and tendering this into evidence, what this proves is that there were cases, possibly many cases, where soldiers were committing offences, perhaps, we don't know, but they were not reporting these offences, and that is a proven fact. Somebody said, oh, yes, I know that this man fired, but he did not report this to his superior, so how do you want this man who has got under his command 20.000 men, how can he know everything that goes right to the bottom of the chain of command? How does he know what a foot soldier is doing if the hierarchy is not reporting this to him. In this case, nothing was reported to General Galic. How can he conduct an investigation if he doesn't know that something has happened. How is that possible? And therefore, how can the Prosecution reproach General Galic for not having carried out investigations? Theoretically this was not possible for him to do. How can -- they can say when investigations were actually proven to have existed, and then the Prosecution says these are quasi investigations, these are just investigations to make them feel better. These were just -- these were just dead pieces of paper that meant nothing. Now, let's go further. We're told that the matchbox building was symbolic, and the Defence has admitted to this fact. Now, fortunately, I now have to subject myself to a returnation of memory. I said -- I don't remember that I said that. I said that was one facility, one building, that could have been important, but I've always said that this was one of the tallest facilities, possibly the tallest facility building in Sarajevo. And it was the top floors that were hit. And the reason why they were hit is probably, almost certainly, these floors were used for -- as firing positions. Now, let us follow to the ground. How do you want a sniper to fire from basement or from lower floors? He's obviously going to take top floors of buildings, and obviously, when we have these top floors attacked, then that is self-explanatory. Wishing to say that these Serb responses against the matchbox or any other buildings would have corresponded to the intent to destroy something that is symbolical, that is simply insulting common sense and logic, because I'm reiterating, if we wish to destroy something that is symbolic, then I'm going to try and destroy something that is extremely important to my opponent. That is going to be something that will hit at the heart of the civilian population, that will hit at the heart of their faith, their religion. I will destroy the museums, the religious facilities. I will destroy what they value most. Again, where is the evidence of that there is none. Let us go back to a hobbyhorse. This is another example that I have to bring up here. When we are told that the shellings can be explained by other things, obviously I am speaking about Wilhem de Kostrowitsky and quoting a different passage, saying that the shells were sounding above the city. And this, we are told, is that we are using the tu quoque defence. Now, if we wanted to use this as tu quoque principle, we were responding because we were being fired at. Or perhaps, I was misunderstood and that I have to take this into account, that there is this possibility that I was misunderstood. But this is false. I have never, the Defence has never said we have a right because of tu quoque, because they fired on us. If ever tu quoque was mentioned, that was in a different context. Legally, the only thing we ever said was if the Prosecution considered that the fact that they themselves believe is established, the shelling of Nedzarici, Ilidza, firing on Grbavica, if all of that is not a violation of the law of war, then tu quoque means for you, too, for you, too, Galic. For the rest, it cannot be; otherwise, it will be very hard to balance two legal terms, terms of justice. So it will be one weight for those who have lost and one for those who have -- who are triumphant. I believe I was very clear. Never has the Defence used tu quoque as a kind of excuse. The simple reason is that the Defence believes that they have a very different excuse that we will try and explain to you. I wish that we heard, maybe that will come, regarding the exchanges of fire. At no point did I have anything that the Prosecution said regarding the changes of fire. We were told no, no, it was a static war. There were no exchanges of fire. How do you imagine that the people were in combat on a daily basis as many witnesses characterise as being a permanent, nonstop combat? There were infantry weapons inside the city, in the streets. There was no street-to-street combat. There were exchanges of fire and there were ricochets. Now, let us go back to the logic. To justify the number of victims in the Markale market, the Prosecution said yes, there were a number of them. You see, there were many ricochets. There were many ricochets because of the metallic structures of the stores, and there were many of them. There were many elements, and this is contradictory but it doesn't matter. The Prosecution tells us, this increased the number of victims because the fragments would ricochet everywhere. But when the Defence says, too, but bullets can ricochet everywhere, suddenly, no, that's not possible. No, if it is exculpatory for General Galic, then it's not possible. These stray bullets, these ricochets, that cannot happen. However, the evidence is that the Prosecution is admitting in the Markale incident that there were many ricochets. And if we say there were many of them, why, why not take them into consideration for the cases that would be exculpatory evidence for General Galic? This is one of those mathematical unknowns that we were talking about. I haven't started the very last minute, Mr. President. I would like to have the famous Tabeau document on the ELMO, if that's possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. With the assistance of Madam Usher, because perhaps I will not be able to thank her again, and now in the few minutes - thank you very much. Look at the very first image. We don't have to zoom at all because we know this very well. The highest line above is the Markale line. So there are two things that are evident here. Never, never before have there been more victims, and we can see that proportionally. Whether they were civilian or military, it doesn't matter. But one should look at this very closely and see the number of victims after February of 1994. So I'm going to this one single question, when we know, and I quoted Mr. Tucker earlier, there was a question at your -- there was an answer at your question, Mr. President. When we know that several UN members had said in the psychological structure, they could imagine, in the mental structure, they could imagine there would be attack against them, there could be the following situation, although we know at the time the Serbs had everything to lose from such an attack. And I'm asking the following question: Isn't it imaginable that someone, no matter who, among the Muslim forces had decided to provoke an intentional sacrifice of several dozens of victims, military and civilian, knowing at that time that the peace will come from there. But not just peace, but the military victory, political victory. And not just in Sarajevo, but in the entire Bosnia. And I know the Prosecution said, oh, well, that is far-fetched. How can one imagine that this was done? People would know about it." So I said "very well. I don't have to be trusted. That's normal." But let's look at history. Let's look at Coventry. Coventry bombed, and Churchill knew, German secret, and he let Coventry be bombed. And this was for strategic reasons that Coventry was bombed -- allowed to be bombed. And this is absolutely possible. Look at this diagram. Look at the figures. One thing: It is certainly not in the Serb interest. That's number one. Number two, isn't it in the Muslim interest? There are many other historical examples where during certain dramatic moments in history, nations decide to sacrifice members of their own nation. Why would that be not the case in Sarajevo equally, and why would that not be the case when one of the parties, and the Defence has proven this, not only this firing happened elsewhere, because Gray did hear, and he repeated what he had heard, but other UN personnel said for the most part that it was among them a commonplace thing that they knew it was atop us [phoen], that Muslim forces could open fire on themselves, and even on the cemeteries. So Mr. President, I think that when one has a look at these figures and one asks what the necessary distance from the events, asks oneself certain questions and one tries to ask oneself the right questions, one asks oneself: Well, what is a campaign, in fact? And if I had the means, because I had the physical means of these weapons, these M84 machine-guns, et cetera. If I have the means to carry out, to implement my campaign, and I allegedly have Sarajevo at my mercy and allegedly in a repeated and systematic manner I fire indiscriminately at civilian areas, well, let's be logical. Wouldn't the extent of damage have been far greater than the extent of damage presented to us? Wouldn't there have been far more civilian victims, far more than the number presented to us? When we compare this on our side, we see that the facts are the same. Isn't this the clearest demonstration of the fact that unfortunately what happened in Sarajevo, the dramatic events that transpired in Sarajevo are exactly the same things that happened on the other side, and this is quite simply called war. However, this is not called a war which is conducted in a criminal and illegitimate manner and within the framework of a campaign the objective of which is to inflict terror on the civilian population. One last matter before I enter into my last minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear your reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Already your last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My very last point is that there is a saying that says "without the body of the crime, in general, there is no crime." Because we can't find it in this case, the body of the crime is terror, the Prosecution has told us. The greatest crime was the crime of spreading terror. And the only thing the Prosecution did not want to prove is the existence of terror. An expert told us the following: "If the circumstances that I am presenting to you are such that they would inflict terror, is terror the result of the circumstances?" And you say that there were circumstances that such terror would be created in such circumstances, then in that case terror is present. There we have a hypothesis. We never convict on the basis of a hypothesis. What we need is certainties, certainties, and certainties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank the flexibility of those assisting us in the technical booth and the interpreters' booth, not only for their flexibility but also for their accuracy they demonstrated us always. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 10.30, Courtroom II. And the parties should then be ready to answer whatever questions the Judges might have. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, how much time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That depends, of course, on the questions of the Judges. And just as the Prosecution would like to have court over now to prepare, we are in an ongoing preparation for our questions. I think it will not take much time. My guess would be not more than one hour, perhaps one hour and 15 minutes. But it always depends on the time the parties take to answer those questions, because as you certainly know, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, eloquence takes time sometimes.
